title: Bios Life leaves stealth with $25M and a Tempus alliance for cancer surveillance
excerpt: Bios Life has emerged from stealth with $25m and a Tempus data alliance to build continuous, AI-driven cancer surveillance for high-risk people and survivors.
content_html:
A team of BioNTech alumni thinks cancer screening has been stuck in the past, and it has raised $25M to do something about it.

Bios Life has emerged from stealth with a plan to replace one-off screening with continuous, AI-driven surveillance, and a data alliance with Tempus to power it.

The seed round is well syndicated for a launch. It was led by Redmile, Vsquared Ventures and Kindred Capital, alongside a group of healthcare and technology investors from across the United States and Europe, giving the Boston company real backing from day one.

The audience it is chasing is large and, it argues, badly served. The company points to more than 40 million Americans who are either cancer survivors or at heightened risk, two groups it says are left with fragmented, reactive care that only kicks in once something has gone wrong.

The stakes it cites are sobering. Bios Life notes that more than 40% of people will be diagnosed with cancer in their lifetime, and that a large share of those diagnoses come late, at stage three or four, when treatment is harder and outcomes worse.

Its answer is a shift from episodes to a continuum. Rather than a scan every year or two, the company wants to maintain what it calls a digital twin for each patient, a continuously updated model of their biology that turns disjointed screening into lifetime monitoring.

Delivery is meant to be virtual-first. Bios Life plans to run the service through an online care platform staffed by licensed clinicians across the US and in partnership with cancer centres, with a launch slated for the second half of 2026 and a waitlist already open.

The technology rests on some serious genomics. The company holds commercial rights to the Nucleotide Transformer, a genomics foundation model from BioNTech-InstaDeep that it says is among the most cited and downloaded in the field, able to read genetic signals down to a single nucleotide.

The Tempus alliance is what gives the models something to learn from. Under the multi-year deal, Bios Life can use Tempus’ de-identified, multi-modal oncology datasets to train and validate its predictive systems, the fuel any medical AI needs to be credible.

Genetics rounds out the picture. Through Tempus-owned Ambry Genetics, a specialist in hereditary cancer testing, Bios Life plans to fold genetic screening into its platform, blending inherited risk with the lifestyle and clinical data it tracks over time.

Its clinical backers frame the moment as overdue. Duke’s Kevin Oeffinger argued that screening has been at a “relative standstill” for decades and that an AI-enhanced virtual model could be a “game changer” for high-risk groups, a strong claim from an academic advisor.

The founders’ pedigree is the pitch’s backbone. Chief executive Ryan Richardson was BioNTech’s chief strategy officer and chaired its AI arm InstaDeep, and he is joined by fellow BioNTech and InstaDeep veterans, the crowd that rode the mRNA and genomics-AI wave.

The technology already spots breast cancer from a scan and, in some studies, has come closer than a biopsy at assessing rare tumours, so the underlying momentum is real.

Founder-led health-AI bets are having a moment, too, with heavyweight operators leaving big jobs to build data-driven medicine of their own, and Bios Life fits that pattern of pedigree meeting patient data.

The caveats, in health especially, deserve top billing. The platform has not launched, AI risk prediction has to be clinically validated before anyone should trust it, and continuous surveillance carries its own hazards, from false alarms and over-screening to the anxiety and cost of chasing findings that may never have mattered.

That is the tension the whole field is living with, where the hype around AI health tech has run ahead of the results.

Bios Life has the team, the data partner and the money; what it has to earn now is proof that lifelong surveillance genuinely helps patients rather than simply watching them more closely.

content_html_zh:
BioNTech 校友团队认为癌症筛查一直停留在过去，他们已经筹集了 2500 万美元来解决这个问题。

Bios Life 已经从秘密中脱颖而出，计划用人工智能驱动的持续监控取代一次性筛查，并与 Tempus 建立数据联盟来为其提供支持。

种子轮融资已顺利启动。 该项目由 Redmile、Vsquared Ventures 和 Kindred Capital 以及来自美国和欧洲各地的一群医疗保健和技术投资者牵头，从第一天起就为这家波士顿公司提供了真正的支持。

它所追逐的观众数量庞大，但他们却得不到很好的服务。 该公司指出，有超过 4000 万美国人要么是癌症幸存者，要么处于高风险状态，该公司表示，这两个群体面临着支离破碎、反应性的护理，只有在出现问题时才会开始实施。

它所提到的利害关系发人深省。 Bios Life 指出，超过 40% 的人会在一生中被诊断出患有癌症，其中很大一部分诊断较晚，即在第三或第四阶段，此时治疗更加困难，结果也更糟糕。

它的答案是从片段到连续体的转变。 该公司希望为每个患者维护一个所谓的数字双胞胎，而不是每年或两年进行一次扫描，这是一个不断更新的生物学模型，可以将脱节的筛查转变为终身监测。

交付应该是虚拟优先的。 Bios Life 计划通过一个由美国各地持证临床医生组成的在线护理平台并与癌症中心合作运行该服务，计划于 2026 年下半年推出，并且已经开放了候补名单。

该技术依赖于一些严肃的基因组学。 该公司拥有 Nucleotide Transformer 的商业权利，这是 BioNTech-InstaDeep 的基因组学基础模型，据称该模型是该领域被引用和下载最多的模型之一，能够读取精确到单个核苷酸的遗传信号。

Tempus 联盟为模型提供了一些值得学习的东西。 根据这项多年协议，Bios Life 可以使用 Tempus 的去识别化、多模式肿瘤学数据集来训练和验证其预测系统，这是任何医疗人工智能可信所需的燃料。

遗传学使情况变得更加圆满。 通过 Tempus 旗下的遗传性癌症检测专家 Ambry Genetics，Bios Life 计划将基因筛查纳入其平台，将遗传风险与其长期跟踪的生活方式和临床数据结合起来。

其临床支持者认为这一时刻早该到来。 杜克大学的凯文·奥芬格 (Kevin Oeffinger) 认为，筛查几十年来一直处于“相对停滞状态”，人工智能增强的虚拟模型可能会成为高风险群体的“游戏规则改变者”，这是一位学术顾问的强烈主张。

创始人的血统是球场的支柱。 首席执行官 Ryan Richardson 是 BioNTech 的首席战略官，并担任其 AI 部门 InstaDeep 的主席，与他一起的还有 BioNTech 和 InstaDeep 的资深人士，他们是 mRNA 和基因组学-AI 浪潮中的一员。

该技术已经通过扫描发现了乳腺癌，并且在一些研究中，在评估罕见肿瘤方面比活检更接近，因此潜在的动力是真实的。

创始人主导的健康人工智能赌注也风靡一时，重量级运营商纷纷辞去重要职位，转而打造自己的数据驱动型医疗，而 Bios Life 符合这种血统与患者数据相结合的模式。

这些注意事项，尤其是在健康方面，值得重点关注。 该平台尚未启动，人工智能风险预测必须经过临床验证才能让任何人相信它，而持续监控也有其自身的危险，从误报和过度筛查到追求可能永远不重要的结果的焦虑和成本。

这就是整个领域面临的紧张局势，围绕人工智能健康技术的炒作已经超过了结果。

Bios Life 有团队、数据合作伙伴和资金；它现在必须获得的证据是，终身监测确实可以帮助患者，而不仅仅是更密切地观察他们。
